title: Anemia: Oxygen Delivery and Cause
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Anemia is reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, not a diagnosis by itself. PN care focuses on symptoms, bleeding or other cause clues, safe activity, medication/nutrition teaching, and escalation for hemodynamic instability, chest pain, syncope, or severe dyspnea.
recognize: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, dizziness, headache, and reduced exercise tolerance are common.
Iron deficiency may be associated with pica or restless legs; acute blood loss can present with hypotension and tachycardia before laboratory values fully reflect loss.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and active bleeding when symptomatic.
Cluster care and pace activity for patients with limited oxygen delivery.
Treat the underlying cause and administer prescribed replacement or transfusion therapy safely.
assessMonitor: Trend symptoms, vital signs, CBC indices, bleeding, stool/urine changes, diet, menstruation history when relevant, and response to therapy.
interventions: Promote rest during severe symptoms while gradually increasing activity as tolerated.
Support iron-rich nutrition when iron deficiency is established.
medicationSafety: Oral iron commonly darkens stool and may cause GI upset/constipation; teach product-specific administration.
Do not assume dark stool is benign when GI bleeding is possible; assess context.
complications: Delayed diagnosis of bleeding or malignancy
teaching: Take replacement therapy for the prescribed duration and return for follow-up testing; correcting the hemoglobin without finding the cause may miss serious disease.
delegationScope: Routine activity assistance may be delegated when stable; new bleeding, dyspnea, chest pain, or syncope requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Telling every patient with anemia simply to eat more iron without identifying whether iron deficiency is actually present.
oneLinePearl: Anemia is a clue—support oxygen delivery and find the cause.
sourceBasis: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute anemia guidance

title: Neutropenic Fever: Infection Emergency
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Fever during significant neutropenia can be the only early sign of a life-threatening infection. Treat it as urgent: assess rapidly, notify the oncology team/provider, obtain ordered cultures/labs without delaying antibiotics, and monitor closely for sepsis.
recognize: Patients with low neutrophil counts may have little pus, redness, or inflammatory response despite serious infection.
Chills, cough, sore throat, diarrhea, dysuria, mouth sores, catheter-site changes, or new malaise may be infection clues.
priorities: Escalate fever or suspected infection immediately.
Use meticulous hand hygiene and infection-prevention measures.
Obtain ordered cultures and administer empiric antimicrobials promptly according to the treatment pathway.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, hemodynamics, mental status, respiratory status, catheter sites, oral mucosa, urine/stool symptoms, and CBC/ANC when available.
interventions: Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories, and unnecessary rectal procedures when neutropenic because mucosal injury can introduce infection.
Use safe food-handling practices rather than unsupported extreme isolation diets.
medicationSafety: Do not mask fever with antipyretics before the oncology team is aware of the episode unless directed.
Monitor renal/hepatic function and infusion reactions with antimicrobial therapy as ordered.
teaching: During neutropenia, follow the oncology team's fever threshold and call immediately rather than waiting to see whether fever resolves.
delegationScope: Vital-sign collection may be delegated, but fever in a neutropenic patient requires licensed-nurse assessment and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for a clearly localized infection before escalating fever in a neutropenic patient.
oneLinePearl: Neutropenia can hide inflammation—fever may be the whole warning.
sourceBasis: National Cancer Institute Infection and Neutropenia guidance

title: Thrombocytopenia: Prevent and Detect Bleeding
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Low platelets increase bleeding risk. Prevent trauma, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures, assess for occult bleeding, and escalate neurologic symptoms or uncontrolled bleeding immediately.
recognize: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, hematuria, melena, or prolonged bleeding may occur.
Sudden headache, confusion, weakness, or vomiting can signal intracranial bleeding.
priorities: Use bleeding precautions appropriate to severity and cause.
Apply prolonged pressure after venipuncture or injections.
Escalate active bleeding or neurologic change.
assessMonitor: Trend platelet count, skin/mucosa, stool/urine, menstrual bleeding when relevant, vital signs, and medication exposures.
interventions: Use a soft toothbrush and electric razor when appropriate.
Avoid rectal procedures and high-trauma activities when bleeding risk is significant.
medicationSafety: Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and other platelet-impairing drugs unless specifically prescribed after risk review.
Confirm whether anticoagulants or heparin exposure could be contributing.
teaching: Report black stools, red urine, prolonged bleeding, severe headache, or falls/head injury promptly.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene may be delegated with bleeding precautions; new bleeding requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving an IM injection or aspirin to a severely thrombocytopenic patient when a safer alternative exists.
oneLinePearl: Low platelets = think bleeding prevention, especially brain and GI tract.

title: Blood Transfusion Reaction: Stop First
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: When a transfusion reaction is suspected, stop the blood product immediately, keep IV access with compatible fluid using new tubing according to policy, assess ABCs/vitals, notify the appropriate team and blood bank, and follow the reaction workup protocol.
recognize: Fever/chills, dyspnea, back or chest pain, hives, hypotension, anxiety, nausea, hemoglobinuria, or sudden respiratory distress can represent a reaction.
TACO and TRALI can both cause respiratory distress but have different mechanisms and management.
priorities: Stop the transfusion.
Assess airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, and vital signs.
Maintain IV access and notify provider/RN/blood bank per policy.
Verify patient/product identification and preserve required blood/tubing specimens per protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory status, temperature, blood pressure, urine output, skin findings, pain, and fluid balance.
interventions: Position and oxygenate as clinically indicated while the cause is evaluated.
Follow facility-specific transfusion-reaction specimen and documentation requirements.
medicationSafety: Do not restart the implicated blood product unless explicitly directed under an established protocol.
Use only compatible IV solutions with blood products according to policy.
teaching: Tell patients to report chills, itching, shortness of breath, chest/back pain, or feeling suddenly unwell during a transfusion.
delegationScope: Transfusion assessment and reaction management remain licensed-nurse responsibilities within state/facility scope; unlicensed personnel should not independently monitor a blood transfusion.
examTrap: Slowing the transfusion and watching instead of stopping it when a reaction is suspected.
oneLinePearl: Transfusion reaction? Stop blood first, then assess and investigate.
sourceBasis: AABB Patient Blood Management Standards 5th edition

title: Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis
bottomLine: Vaso-occlusive crisis causes severe ischemic pain and requires rapid analgesia, assessment for dangerous complications, hydration when indicated, and oxygen only for hypoxemia—not reflexively for every pain crisis.
recognize: Severe bone, joint, chest, abdominal, or back pain may occur without visible injury.
Fever, respiratory symptoms, neurologic deficits, priapism, or enlarging spleen change the urgency and differential.
priorities: Assess pain promptly and administer prescribed analgesia without stigmatizing delay.
Check oxygenation, temperature, respiratory status, neurologic status, and hydration.
Escalate possible acute chest syndrome, stroke, infection, splenic sequestration, or priapism.
assessMonitor: Trend pain response, sedation/respiratory status, SpO2, fever, hydration, CBC/reticulocyte data when ordered, and new chest or neurologic symptoms.
interventions: Encourage incentive spirometry in hospitalized patients when ordered/appropriate to reduce pulmonary complications.
Use individualized hydration rather than indiscriminate large fluid boluses.
medicationSafety: Opioids often are necessary for severe crisis pain; monitor respiratory status while avoiding undertreatment.
NSAID use depends on renal function, bleeding risk, and the treatment plan.
redFlags: Chest pain with fever or hypoxemia
teaching: Maintain hydration, use prescribed disease-modifying therapy, avoid known triggers when possible, and seek urgent care for fever, chest symptoms, neurologic changes, or prolonged priapism.
delegationScope: Routine comfort measures may be delegated, but new respiratory, neurologic, or hemodynamic changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming severe reported pain is drug-seeking behavior or giving oxygen despite normal oxygenation while missing acute chest symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Treat the pain fast—and keep looking for chest, brain, spleen, and infection emergencies.
sourceBasis: 2025 emergency and critical illness sickle cell guidance

title: Preoperative Safety and Consent
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Before surgery, verify identity, procedure/site, allergies, NPO/medication instructions, required preparation, and that informed consent has been completed by the responsible provider. The nurse witnesses the signature and assesses voluntariness/understanding within role; the nurse does not independently provide the surgeon's procedural consent explanation.
recognize: Anticoagulants, diabetes medications, implanted devices, pregnancy possibility, allergies, previous anesthesia problems, and difficult airway history may alter perioperative planning.
priorities: Verify patient, procedure, site, and consent status before premedication or transfer.
Report unanswered questions or apparent misunderstanding before surgery proceeds.
Confirm medication holds/administration using current orders rather than assumptions.
assessMonitor: Assess baseline vital signs, pain, skin, mobility, airway-related history, medication list, allergies, and psychosocial concerns.
interventions: Remove items and complete preparation according to the procedure and policy.
Protect privacy, valuables, dentures/hearing aids/glasses according to the perioperative plan.
medicationSafety: Do not give sedating preoperative medication before unresolved consent questions are addressed.
Diabetes and anticoagulant plans must be individualized to the procedure and orders.
redFlags: New chest pain or unstable vital signs
teaching: Explain what the patient can expect from nursing preparation and recovery while directing procedure-specific risk questions to the qualified procedural provider.
delegationScope: Consent verification and preoperative assessment are licensed-nurse responsibilities; clerical preparation does not replace clinical verification.
examTrap: Asking a sedated patient to sign a consent or personally explaining risks that should be addressed by the procedural provider.
oneLinePearl: No unresolved consent, identity, site, or medication issue goes to the OR.

title: Postoperative Atelectasis and Pulmonary Prevention
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: After surgery, shallow breathing, pain, immobility, and sedation promote atelectasis. Priorities are adequate analgesia, upright positioning, coughing/deep breathing, incentive spirometry when prescribed, and early mobilization while monitoring for pneumonia, PE, opioid oversedation, or other causes of hypoxemia.
recognize: Diminished dependent breath sounds, mild hypoxemia, tachypnea, and poor inspiratory effort may occur.
Sudden severe dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, unilateral leg swelling, or marked hypoxemia suggests PE rather than routine atelectasis.
priorities: Assess respiratory rate, effort, lung sounds, oxygenation, sedation, and pain.
Position upright and mobilize early when safe.
Coach deep breathing/coughing and prescribed incentive spirometry.
assessMonitor: Trend SpO2, sedation, respiratory rate, temperature, sputum, breath sounds, mobility, and opioid exposure.
interventions: Splint abdominal/thoracic incisions during cough as appropriate.
Coordinate analgesia before pulmonary exercises and ambulation.
medicationSafety: Excess opioids can worsen hypoventilation; assess sedation and respiratory status rather than treating pain score in isolation.
teaching: Frequent movement and lung-expansion exercises are part of recovery, not optional extras.
delegationScope: Ambulation and incentive-spirometry reinforcement may be delegated for stable patients after the plan is established; deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Automatically labeling every postoperative fever or low oxygen saturation as atelectasis without evaluating infection, PE, aspiration, or opioid effect.
oneLinePearl: Pain control + upright lungs + movement prevents many postoperative pulmonary problems.

title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
bottomLine: Sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision or halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, a red eye, and a fixed or mid-dilated pupil can indicate acute angle closure. This is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate pressure-lowering treatment and definitive ophthalmologic care.
recognize: Symptoms often appear abruptly and may be mistaken for migraine or GI illness because nausea/vomiting can be prominent.
The cornea may appear hazy and vision can decline rapidly.
priorities: Escalate immediately for urgent ophthalmologic management.
Assess visual symptoms and avoid delaying care for routine eye testing.
Administer ordered pressure-lowering medications promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend visual acuity when possible, pain, nausea, pupil findings, vital signs, medication exposure, and response to treatment.
interventions: Reduce environmental hazards because vision may be impaired.
Prepare for definitive laser peripheral iridotomy when indicated.
medicationSafety: Certain anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drugs can precipitate angle closure in susceptible patients; report recent medication exposure.
teaching: Seek emergency care for sudden painful red eye with visual change rather than waiting for a routine eye appointment.
delegationScope: Acute visual loss or severe eye pain requires licensed-nurse assessment and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating sudden painful red eye as conjunctivitis.
oneLinePearl: Painful red eye + halos + nausea = pressure emergency.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology acute angle-closure guidance

title: Cataract Care and Postoperative Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cataracts cause painless progressive lens clouding and reduced vision. After cataract surgery, protect the eye, administer drops correctly, reduce fall risk, and report sudden pain, vision loss, flashes/floaters, increasing redness, or discharge promptly.
recognize: Glare, halos, faded colors, decreased night vision, and gradual painless blurring are common.
Sudden severe pain or abrupt vision loss is not an expected cataract symptom.
priorities: Promote safe mobility and lighting before treatment.
After surgery, prevent eye trauma/rubbing and follow activity restrictions.
Administer prescribed topical medications using clean technique.
assessMonitor: Assess vision changes, falls, ability to self-administer drops, postoperative pain, redness, drainage, and adherence.
interventions: Use assistive devices and environmental modifications as needed.
Separate multiple eye drops by the instructed interval to avoid washing one out.
medicationSafety: Use punctal occlusion when instructed to reduce systemic absorption of certain ophthalmic medications.
redFlags: New flashes/floaters or curtain-like vision loss
teaching: Use prescribed eye protection and activity restrictions and keep follow-up appointments even if vision improves quickly.
delegationScope: Routine assistance may be delegated; postoperative red-flag symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring a postoperative cataract patient that severe eye pain is expected.
oneLinePearl: Cataracts are painless and gradual; sudden pain or vision loss is something else.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Ophthalmology cataract guidance

title: Hearing Loss: Communicate for Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Hearing impairment can look like confusion or nonadherence when the real problem is communication access. Optimize hearing devices and environment, face the patient, speak clearly without shouting, verify understanding, and obtain qualified interpretation/communication support when needed.
recognize: Patients may answer inappropriately, withdraw, watch lips closely, or repeatedly ask for repetition.
Cerumen, medication effects, infection, sudden sensorineural loss, and chronic age-related loss have different implications.
priorities: Confirm hearing aids are present, functioning, and safely stored when removed.
Reduce background noise and face the patient in good light.
Escalate sudden unilateral hearing loss because time-sensitive evaluation may be needed.
assessMonitor: Assess onset, laterality, associated vertigo/tinnitus/pain, medication exposures, cognition after communication is optimized, and device function.
interventions: Use written or visual reinforcement as appropriate.
Use teach-back rather than assuming nodding means understanding.
medicationSafety: Review potentially ototoxic medications when new hearing changes occur and report concerns rather than discontinuing therapy independently.
redFlags: Hearing loss with focal neurologic deficits
teaching: Protect hearing from excessive noise and maintain hearing devices according to manufacturer/audiology instructions.
delegationScope: Communication accommodations are everyone's responsibility; sudden changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Shouting from across the room or assuming the patient is confused before fixing the communication barrier.
oneLinePearl: Face the patient, reduce noise, verify understanding—and never mistake hearing loss for confusion.
